chief_complaint: coughing up bright red blood, shortness of breath, and dark brown urine for 2 weeks
hpi_details: 2-week history of rapidly worsening shortness of breath accompanied by a persistent cough that is now expectorating daily quantities of bright red, pure blood (frank haemoptysis up to 50-100 mL daily). Over the same timeframe, has experienced profound, exhausting fatigue, low-grade fevers, pale skin, and noticed her urine turning dark, smoky brown/red ('Coca-Cola coloured' urine) with noticeable reduction in daily urine output (oliguria). Noticeably, she reports completely normal nasal sinuses, zero nasal crusting, zero ear pains, and zero joint pains. Previously healthy until a mild flu-like upper respiratory illness 4 weeks ago. Never smoked.
ideas: thinks the flu virus attacked the blood vessel walls in both her lungs and kidneys simultaneously
concerns: terrified she will bleed to death inside her lungs or require emergency kidney dialysis
expectations: wants specific basement membrane antibody blood tests, emergency plasma cleaning, and high-dose IV steroids
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, primary school teacher, married

investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent results show diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with rapidly progressive kidney injury; critical-care and nephrology involvement should not await serology or biopsy.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Anti-GBM Disease (Goodpasture Syndrome) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Goodpasture's Syndrome (Anti-GBM Disease -> Type II hypersensitivity autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Medical and nephrological emergency requiring immediate ICU admission and respiratory support, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: coughing up bright red blood, shortness of breath, and dark brown urine for 2 weeks

Key HPI features: 2-week history of rapidly worsening shortness of breath accompanied by a persistent cough that is now expectorating daily quantities of bright red, pure blood (frank haemoptysis up to 50-100 mL daily). Over the same timeframe, has experienced profound, exhausting fatigue, low-grade fevers, pale skin, and noticed her urine turning dark, smoky brown/red ('Coca-Cola coloured' urine) with noticeable reduction in daily urine output (oliguria). Noticeably, she reports completely normal nasal sinuses, zero nasal crusting, zero ear pains, and zero joint pains. Previously healthy until a mild flu-like upper respiratory illness 4 weeks ago. Never smoked.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform targeted emergency physical examination. Vitals: tachypnoea RR 26, tachycardia HR 112, O2 sat 90% on room air, marked conjunctival and facial pallor. ENT/Upper airway exam: completely normal nasal septum without crusting or saddle-nose deformity (critical distinction from GPA). Chest auscultation: widespread bilateral inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields indicating Diffuse Alveolar Haemorrhage. Dipstick urinalysis: 4+ blood and 3+ protein. Urine microscopy: abundant Red Blood Cell Casts and dysmorphic RBCs confirming acute glomerulonephritis. Bloods: severe normocytic anaemia (Hb 72 g/L secondary to pulmonary haemorrhage), serum creatinine markedly elevated (creatinine 420 umol/L confirming rapidly progressive renal failure). CRITICAL AUTOANTIBODY SEROLOGY: check Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane (Anti-GBM antibodies -> markedly positive high titre directed against the non-collagenous NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen). Check ANCA (negative, though 20-30% of patients can be double-positive). Chest X-ray and HRCT Chest: reveals bilateral, symmetrical, alveolar bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation radiating from the hila ('bat-wing' appearance) sparing the apices, typical of acute alveolar haemorrhage. Urgent Renal Biopsy: confirms Crescentric Glomerulonephritis with pathognomonic LINEAR IgG and C3 deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Goodpasture's Syndrome (Anti-GBM Disease -> Type II hypersensitivity autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Community-acquired pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90%).
management_principles: Medical and nephrological emergency requiring immediate ICU admission and respiratory support
Remission-induction treatment is selected urgently by nephrology and rheumatology after diagnostic and infection assessment.
Plasma exchange may be considered by the specialist team for selected severe presentations.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 44F presents with acute 2-week pulmonary-renal syndrome: frank haemoptysis, progressive dyspnoea, oliguria, and macroscopic haematuria, WITHOUT upper airway/sinus involvement.
reference_soap.objective: Perform targeted emergency physical examination. Vitals: tachypnoea RR 26, tachycardia HR 112, O2 sat 90% on room air, marked conjunctival and facial pallor. ENT/Upper airway exam: completely normal nasal septum without crusting or saddle-nose deformity (critical distinction from GPA). Chest auscultation: widespread bilateral inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields indicating Diffuse Alveolar Haemorrhage. Dipstick urinalysis: 4+ blood and 3+ protein. Urine microscopy: abundant Red Blood Cell Casts and dysmorphic RBCs confirming acute glomerulonephritis. Bloods: severe normocytic anaemia (Hb 72 g/L secondary to pulmonary haemorrhage), serum creatinine markedly elevated (creatinine 420 umol/L confirming rapidly progressive renal failure). CRITICAL AUTOANTIBODY SEROLOGY: check Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane (Anti-GBM antibodies -> markedly positive high titre directed against the non-collagenous NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen). Check ANCA (negative, though 20-30% of patients can be double-positive). Chest X-ray and HRCT Chest: reveals bilateral, symmetrical, alveolar bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation radiating from the hila ('bat-wing' appearance) sparing the apices, typical of acute alveolar haemorrhage. Urgent Renal Biopsy: confirms Crescentric Glomerulonephritis with pathognomonic LINEAR IgG and C3 deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence.
reference_soap.assessment: Goodpasture's Syndrome (Anti-GBM Disease -> Type II hypersensitivity autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome). DDx: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA -> shows c-ANCA/anti-PR3 positive, destructive upper sinus/nasal disease, and pauci-immune renal immunofluorescence), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA -> p-ANCA positive, pauci-immune), Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (shows granular immune complex deposition), idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis.
reference_soap.plan: This is a medical and nephrological emergency: admit urgently and involve nephrology, respiratory, and critical-care teams. Monitor gas exchange, haemoglobin, renal function, urine output, and haemodynamics; confirm anti-GBM disease with appropriate serology and biopsy when safe while excluding infection and other pulmonary-renal syndromes. The specialist team may initiate immunosuppression and consider plasma exchange or renal-replacement/ventilatory support according to severity, contraindications, and local protocols.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Goodpasture's Syndrome from Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis based on complete absence of upper airway sinus/nasal necrosis and specific autoantibody targets
Correlate circulating Anti-GBM antibodies targeting Type IV collagen with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Recognize the need for urgent specialist-directed immunosuppression and consideration of plasma exchange in severe anti-GBM disease
Monitor serial hemoglobin and arterial blood gases to catch catastrophic diffuse alveolar haemorrhage mandating early mechanical ventilation

teaching.one_liner: Pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis suggests an anti-GBM pulmonary-renal syndrome.
differentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmonary-renal syndrome

must_ask.say: How much blood have you been coughing up each day, and how quickly did this start?
Have you noticed your urine turning dark or brown, or passing less urine than usual?

must_ask.objective: Absence of ENT symptoms to distinguish from GPA
must_ask.say: Have you had any sinus problems, nosebleeds, or ear pain with this illness?

must_ask.objective: Preceding viral illness or exposure trigger
must_ask.say: Did you have a cold or flu-like illness in the weeks before this started?

must_ask.objective: Anti-GBM antibody and renal biopsy workup
must_ask.say: We'll need urgent blood tests for a specific antibody and likely a kidney biopsy to confirm this.

history.answer: Doctor, I've been coughing up bright red blood and feeling terribly short of breath for the past two weeks, and my urine has turned dark brown.
The blood definitely comes straight from my lungs when I cough; I haven't been vomiting or having any nosebleeds.
It started as small spatters, but over the last week it has increased to about half a cup of pure blood every day.
It is bright red, pure liquid blood, and there is no food or stomach acid mixed in it.
It began about two weeks ago and has been getting steadily heavier and more alarming each day.
I developed an irritating dry cough about two weeks ago right before the bleeding began, but I had no chronic cough before that.
No, I've never coughed up thick yellow phlegm or bad-smelling mucus, and I haven't had recurrent chest infections.
I have had mild low-grade fevers and felt warm on and off, but I haven't had any severe shaking chills.
I haven't lost weight or had night sweats, but I have felt completely exhausted and weak for the past two weeks.
I've become severely short of breath just walking across a room, but I don't feel any sharp or stabbing chest pain when breathing.
No, neither leg is swollen or tender, and I haven't had any surgery, long-distance travel, or prolonged bed rest.
I don't have trouble breathing when lying flat, I don't wake up gasping at night, and my feet aren't swollen.
No, I don't have any sinus pain, nasal congestion, nosebleeds, or bloody crusts inside my nose.
No, I haven't had any ear pain, hearing trouble, or aching and swollen joints.
My urine turned dark and smoky, almost like Coca-Cola, two weeks ago, and I've noticed I'm peeing far less than usual.
No, I haven't had any bleeding from my gums, unusual bruising on my skin, or blood thinners.
No nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, heartburn, or black stools whatsoever.
I had a mild flu with a runny nose and muscle aches about four weeks ago, but that went away before this started.
I've never had tuberculosis and have never been around anyone sick with it.
I haven't traveled abroad recently, and I work as an elementary school teacher, so I haven't breathed in chemical fumes or dust.
I was wondering if that flu virus a month ago somehow damaged the blood vessels in both my lungs and kidneys.
I'm terrified that I might bleed to death inside my lungs, or that my kidneys are shutting down and I'll need dialysis.
I have always been completely healthy with no high blood pressure, asthma, or kidney trouble.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medicines, just paracetamol as needed over the past two weeks for the fever.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I don't drink any alcohol.
I teach primary school and live at home with my husband.
There is no family history of kidney failure, lung hemorrhage, or autoimmune diseases.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles have always been regular.
There is no chance I am pregnant; my husband and I use barrier contraception.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 90% on room air.
Acutely ill-appearing female with prominent facial pallor, sitting upright with labored respirations.
Marked conjunctival pallor bilaterally; sclerae are anicteric.
Nasal mucosa is intact without ulcers, crusting, perforation, or saddle-nose deformity; posterior pharynx is clear with no active bleeding.
No tenderness elicited over the frontal or maxillary sinuses.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Jugular venous pulsation is visible at 2 cm above the sternal angle with no jugular venous distention.
Symmetrical resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields.
Widespread bilateral inspiratory fine crackles throughout both lung bases and mid-zones without wheezing.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without guarding or palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion bilaterally.
No peripheral edema in the lower extremities; no digital clubbing.
Calves are supple, symmetric, and non-tender without swelling, warmth, or cord sign.
Generalized pallor without petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, or vasculitic skin lesions.
